title: Oxidation, reduction and oxidation states
html:
Guiding question

Guiding question: What happens when electrons are transferred?

Redox reactions are reactions in which electrons move from one species to another. They power batteries and fuel cells, are driven backwards by electricity in electrolysis, extract metals from ores, cause corrosion, and change one organic functional group into another. The key skill throughout is tracking electrons – with oxidation states and half-equations.

R3.2.1 Oxidation, reduction and oxidation states

Oxidation and reduction were first defined in terms of oxygen. The modern definitions are about electrons; the older ones still appear, especially in organic chemistry.

OxidationReduction
Electronsloss of electronsgain of electrons
Oxidation stateincreasedecrease
Oxygengain of oxygenloss of oxygen
Hydrogenloss of hydrogengain of hydrogen
Key pointOIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain (of electrons). Oxidation and reduction always happen together – electrons lost by one species must be gained by another – hence red-ox. The more easily a substance loses electrons, the more easily it is oxidized; the more easily it gains them, the more easily it is reduced.
DefinitionAn oxidizing agent (oxidant) accepts electrons from another species and is itself reduced. A reducing agent (reductant) donates electrons to another species and is itself oxidized.

Rather than hunting for electrons, it is usually easier to compare oxidation states. Every element in a compound is given one: if it increases, that element has been oxidized; if it decreases, it has been reduced.

Oxidation state is the charge an atom would have if all its bonds were fully ionic. Rules (apply in this order):

  1. Uncombined element: 0 (Na, O₂, S₈, Cl₂).
  2. Monatomic ion: equal to its charge (Fe³⁺ = +3, Cl⁻ = −1).
  3. Sum of oxidation states = 0 in a neutral compound, or = the charge of a polyatomic ion.
  4. F is always −1. Group 1 = +1, group 2 = +2, Al = +3 in compounds.
  5. H is +1, except in metal hydrides (NaH, LiAlH₄) where it is −1.
  6. O is −2, except in peroxides (H₂O₂, Na₂O₂) where it is −1 and in OF₂ where it is +2.
  7. In binary compounds, the more electronegative element takes its usual negative value (Cl −1 except when bonded to O or F).
Worked exampleFind the oxidation state of the named element.
  • PbCl₄: 4 × (−1) = −4, so Pb = +4.
  • CO₃²⁻: 3 × (−2) = −6; total −2, so C = +4.
  • Cl₂O₃ (covalent – careful, it is not ionic): 3 × (−2) = −6; two Cl share +6, so Cl = +3.
  • Cr₂O₇²⁻: 7 × (−2) = −14; total −2, so 2Cr = +12, Cr = +6.
  • NH₄Cl: N = −3, H = +1, Cl = −1. SOCl₂: S = +4.
Practice: give the oxidation state of each element in CH₄, PCl₃, NCl₃, CS₂, ICl₅, BrF₃, PCl₄⁺, H₃PO₄, H₂SO₄, MgCO₃
SpeciesOxidation states
CH₄C −4, H +1
PCl₃P +3, Cl −1
NCl₃N +3, Cl −1 (N and Cl have similar electronegativity; by convention Cl is −1)
CS₂C +4, S −2
ICl₅I +5, Cl −1
BrF₃Br +3, F −1
PCl₄⁺P +5, Cl −1
H₃PO₄P +5, H +1, O −2
H₂SO₄S +6, H +1, O −2
MgCO₃Mg +2, C +4, O −2

What is the oxidation state of sulfur in the thiosulfate ion, S₂O₃²⁻?

3 × (−2) = −6; total −2, so 2S = +4 and each S = +2 (an average).

In which species does oxygen have an oxidation state of −1?

  1. H₂O
  2. Na₂O₂
  3. OF₂
  4. O₃

Na₂O₂ is a peroxide (O–O bond), so each O is −1. In H₂O it is −2, in OF₂ +2 (F is more electronegative), and in the element O₃ it is 0.

Oxidation states are written as sign then number (+3); charges as number then sign (3+). Roman numerals in names give the oxidation state (IUPAC calls this the oxidation number): iron(III) chloride FeCl₃, manganese(IV) oxide MnO₂, sulfur(VI) oxide SO₃, dichromate(VI) Cr₂O₇²⁻, phosphorus(V) chloride PCl₅, phosphorus(III) chloride PCl₃, lead(IV) oxide PbO₂, tin(II) chloride SnCl₂. They are used for any element that can have more than one oxidation state, not only transition metals.

Name: PbO₂, SnCl₂, SbCl₃, TiCl₄, BrF₅

lead(IV) oxide; tin(II) chloride; antimony(III) chloride; titanium(IV) chloride; bromine(V) fluoride.

A reaction is redox only if oxidation states change. Neutralization and precipitation reactions are not redox.

Which reaction is not a redox reaction?

  1. Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂
  2. Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂
  3. CuO + 2HCl → CuCl₂ + H₂O
  4. Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaOCl + H₂O

In CuO + 2HCl, Cu stays +2, O −2, H +1 and Cl −1: an acid–base reaction. The others all have changes (Mg 0 → +2; Fe +3 → 0; Cl 0 → −1 and +1).

In disproportionation the same element is simultaneously oxidized and reduced, e.g. Cl₂ + H₂O → HCl + HOCl (Cl: 0 → −1 and 0 → +1); 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂ (O: −1 → −2 and −1 → 0); Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaOCl + H₂O (Cl: 0 → −1 and 0 → +1).

title: Half-equations and balancing redox equations
html:
R3.2.2 Half-equations and balancing redox equations

It can be difficult to see what is oxidized and what is reduced in a full equation. A half-equation shows either the oxidation or the reduction on its own, with electrons included. Electrons appear on the right for oxidation and on the left for reduction.

oxidation: Zn(s) → Zn²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻     reduction: Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ → Cu(s)

So H₂ → 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ (oxidation: electrons lost) and F₂ + 2e⁻ → 2F⁻ (reduction: electrons gained). Adding the two half-equations, the electrons cancel and give back the ionic equation F₂ + H₂ → 2F⁻ + 2H⁺.

Balancing a half-equation in acidic solution (the method examiners expect):

  1. Balance the element that changes oxidation state.
  2. Balance O by adding H₂O.
  3. Balance H by adding H⁺.
  4. Balance charge by adding electrons to the more positive side.
Worked exampleAcidified manganate(VII) oxidizes Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺. Write the overall equation.
  1. Reduction: MnO₄⁻ → Mn²⁺. Add 4H₂O on the right for O: MnO₄⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O. Add 8H⁺ on the left: MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O. Charge: left +7, right +2, so add 5e⁻ on the left:
    MnO₄⁻(aq) + 8H⁺(aq) + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺(aq) + 4H₂O(l)
  2. Oxidation: Fe²⁺(aq) → Fe³⁺(aq) + e⁻
  3. Equalize electrons: multiply the oxidation by 5, add, cancel electrons:
    MnO₄⁻(aq) + 8H⁺(aq) + 5Fe²⁺(aq) → Mn²⁺(aq) + 4H₂O(l) + 5Fe³⁺(aq)
  4. Check: atoms balance and charge is +17 on both sides.
Worked exampleHydrogen peroxide oxidizes iodide ions in acid: 2KI + 2HCl + H₂O₂ → I₂ + 2H₂O + 2KCl.
  • Rewrite as ions and cross out the spectators (K⁺ and Cl⁻): 2I⁻ + 2H⁺ + H₂O₂ → I₂ + 2H₂O.
  • Oxidation: 2I⁻(aq) → I₂(aq) + 2e⁻
  • Reduction: H₂O₂ → 2H₂O is unbalanced for H; 2H⁺ + H₂O₂ → 2H₂O is unbalanced for charge; so H₂O₂(aq) + 2H⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ → 2H₂O(l)
  • Overall: H₂O₂(aq) + 2H⁺(aq) + 2I⁻(aq) → I₂(aq) + 2H₂O(l)
Iodine/thiosulfate (used in redox titrations): I₂ + 2e⁻ → 2I⁻ and 2S₂O₃²⁻ → S₄O₆²⁻ + 2e⁻, giving I₂ + 2S₂O₃²⁻ → 2I⁻ + S₄O₆²⁻ (Na⁺ is the spectator ion not shown).
Common mistakeNever leave electrons in an overall equation, and never balance a half-equation by adding O₂ or H₂ – use H₂O and H⁺. Remove spectator ions (K⁺, Na⁺, Cl⁻, SO₄²⁻ that do not change) before writing ionic equations.

Know the difference between a chemical equation (all formulae, e.g. 2KI + 2HCl + H₂O₂ → …), an ionic equation (spectators removed) and an ionic half-equation (one process, with electrons). In exams you are usually asked to build the half-equations first and then combine them.

Which is the correctly balanced half-equation for the reduction of Cr₂O₇²⁻ to Cr³⁺ in acid?

  1. Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6e⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O
  2. Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O + 6e⁻
  3. Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 7H⁺ + 3e⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O
  4. Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 3e⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O

Cr goes from +6 to +3, so 2 Cr gain 6 electrons in total. Charge: left −2 + 14 − 6 = +6; right 2 × (+3) = +6. Electrons on the left = reduction.

What is the oxidation half-equation in 2S₂O₃²⁻(aq) + I₂(aq) → S₄O₆²⁻(aq) + 2I⁻(aq)?

  1. I₂ + 2e⁻ → 2I⁻
  2. 2I⁻ → I₂ + 2e⁻
  3. 2S₂O₃²⁻ → S₄O₆²⁻ + 2e⁻
  4. S₄O₆²⁻ + 2e⁻ → 2S₂O₃²⁻

Thiosulfate loses electrons (S: +2 → +2.5 on average), so it is oxidized. I₂ + 2e⁻ → 2I⁻ is the reduction; the other two are the reverse reactions.

Write half-equations: (a) Pb⁴⁺ → Pb²⁺ (b) Br⁻ → Br₂ (c) SO₄²⁻ → S (d) SO₄²⁻ → H₂S (e) N₂ → NO₃⁻ (f) IO₃⁻ → I₂ (g) NO₃⁻ → NO₂
  1. Pb⁴⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb²⁺
  2. 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻
  3. SO₄²⁻ + 8H⁺ + 6e⁻ → S + 4H₂O
  4. SO₄²⁻ + 10H⁺ + 8e⁻ → H₂S + 4H₂O
  5. N₂ + 6H₂O → 2NO₃⁻ + 12H⁺ + 10e⁻
  6. 2IO₃⁻ + 12H⁺ + 10e⁻ → I₂ + 6H₂O
  7. NO₃⁻ + 2H⁺ + e⁻ → NO₂ + H₂O
Combine to give the overall equation: MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O with 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻

Multiply the first by 2 and the second by 5 (10 electrons each): 2MnO₄⁻ + 16H⁺ + 10Cl⁻ → 2Mn²⁺ + 8H₂O + 5Cl₂.

Combine: 2IO₃⁻ + 12H⁺ + 10e⁻ → I₂ + 6H₂O with 2I⁻ → I₂ + 2e⁻

Multiply the second by 5: 2IO₃⁻ + 10I⁻ + 12H⁺ → 6I₂ + 6H₂O (an example of comproportionation: I from +5 and −1 both end at 0).

Magnetite, Fe₃O₄, contains both Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺. How many Fe³⁺ ions are there for each Fe²⁺ ion?

Total positive charge must be +8 (4 × O²⁻ = −8). With 3 Fe: x(+2) + (3 − x)(+3) = 8 gives x = 1. So 1 Fe²⁺ : 2 Fe³⁺.

title: Reactivity: ease of oxidation, activity series and metals with acids
html:
R3.2.3 Relative ease of oxidation and reduction of elements

How easily an atom loses or gains electrons depends on atomic radius, nuclear charge and shielding by inner electrons.

  • Metals lose electrons to form cations, so they tend to be oxidized and act as reducing agents. Down group 1 (Li → Cs) the outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded, so it is lost more easily: reactivity and reducing strength increase down the group (e.g. reaction with water: Li fizzes steadily, K ignites).
  • Non-metals such as halogens gain electrons to form anions, so they tend to be reduced and act as oxidizing agents. Up group 17 the atom is smaller, so an incoming electron is attracted more strongly by the nucleus: oxidizing strength increases up the group (F₂ > Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂).

Demonstration: alkali metals with water

2Li(s) + 2H₂O(l) → 2LiOH(aq) + H₂(g)    Li: 0 → +1 (oxidized); H: +1 → 0 (reduced)

A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive halide from solution:

Cl₂(aq) + 2Br⁻(aq) → 2Cl⁻(aq) + Br₂(aq)    (colourless → orange/yellow)

Which mixture would react?

  1. I₂(aq) + KBr(aq)
  2. Br₂(aq) + KCl(aq)
  3. Br₂(aq) + KI(aq)
  4. I₂(aq) + KCl(aq)

Br₂ is a stronger oxidizing agent than I₂ (smaller atom), so it oxidizes I⁻ to I₂: Br₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Br⁻ + I₂ (solution turns brown). A halogen cannot oxidize the halide of a more reactive halogen.

The activity series ranks metals by how easily they are oxidized: K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > (C) > Zn > Fe > Sn > Pb > (H) > Cu > Ag > Au. One mnemonic: "Please Stop Calling Me A Careless Zebra Instead Try Learning How Copper Saves Gold". A metal displaces any metal below it from a solution of its ions:

Fe(s) + CuSO₄(aq) → FeSO₄(aq) + Cu(s)    ionic: Fe(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Fe²⁺(aq) + Cu(s)

The activity series is given in the data booklet.

Which metal would displace zinc from zinc sulfate solution?

  1. Copper
  2. Iron
  3. Magnesium
  4. Lead

Only a metal above zinc in the activity series (more easily oxidized) can reduce Zn²⁺. Magnesium is above zinc; Fe, Pb and Cu are below it.

R3.2.4 Reactions of metals with acids

Metals above hydrogen in the activity series react with dilute acids, releasing hydrogen. This is a redox reaction: the metal is oxidized and H⁺ is reduced. (Neutralization – acid + base – is not redox.)

Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g)    ionic: Mg(s) + 2H⁺(aq) → Mg²⁺(aq) + H₂(g)
  • Observations: effervescence, metal dissolves, test gas with a lighted splint → squeaky pop.
  • Metals below hydrogen (Cu, Ag, Au) do not react with dilute non-oxidizing acids.
  • The higher the metal is in the series, the more vigorous the reaction.

Name the salt from the acid: H₂SO₄ → sulfate (SO₄²⁻), HCl → chloride (Cl⁻), HNO₃ → nitrate (NO₃⁻). Charges of the metal ions come from the group number (or the Roman numeral for transition metals), and the formula must have zero overall charge.

Write the ionic equation for zinc with sulfuric acid and identify the oxidizing agent.

Zn(s) + 2H⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + H₂(g). SO₄²⁻ is a spectator. Zn: 0 → +2 (oxidized, reducing agent); H: +1 → 0 (reduced), so H⁺ is the oxidizing agent.

Which metal does not react with dilute hydrochloric acid?

  1. Zinc
  2. Iron
  3. Copper
  4. Magnesium

Copper is below hydrogen in the activity series, so it cannot reduce H⁺ to H₂.

title: Voltaic, primary, secondary and electrolytic cells
html:
R3.2.5 Voltaic (galvanic) cells

DefinitionA voltaic cell converts chemical energy from a spontaneous redox reaction into electrical energy. Oxidation and reduction happen in separate half-cells, so electrons are forced to travel through an external wire.

A half-cell is a metal dipped in a solution of its own ions, e.g. Zn(s) in Zn²⁺(aq), where an equilibrium Zn²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ ⇌ Zn(s) is set up. The position of this equilibrium tells us how readily the metal releases electrons – how good a reducing agent it is. The potential of a single half-cell cannot be measured; only the potential difference between two half-cells can, using a high-resistance voltmeter.

Daniell cell (Zn | Zn²⁺ and Cu²⁺ | Cu):

  • Zinc is more reactive, so it is oxidized: Zn(s) → Zn²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻. This electrode is the anode and is the negative electrode.
  • Electrons flow through the wire to copper, where Cu²⁺ is reduced: Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ → Cu(s). This electrode is the cathode and is positive.
  • Overall: Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s); E = +1.10 V under standard conditions.
  • Observations over time: zinc electrode loses mass, copper electrode gains mass, blue colour of Cu²⁺ fades.

The salt bridge (filter paper or a tube soaked in e.g. KNO₃(aq)) completes the circuit by allowing ions to move between the half-cells, keeping each solution electrically neutral. Anions move towards the anode half-cell (where positive Zn²⁺ ions are building up) and cations towards the cathode half-cell. Its ions must not react with the electrodes or solutions (KCl is unsuitable with Ag⁺ because AgCl would precipitate, and chloride ions can also form complexes with copper ions).

Key pointElectrons flow through the wire, from anode (−) to cathode (+). Ions flow through the salt bridge and solutions. Electrons never pass through the salt bridge or the solution. Mnemonic: An Ox, Red Cat – oxidation at the anode, reduction at the cathode (true for every type of cell).
Common mistakeIt is the more reactive metal that is oxidized, so it is the anode; the less reactive metal's ions are reduced at the cathode. Do not swap these. Also, metals in half-equations are solids: Zn(s), Cu(s), not (aq).

Cell diagram (IUPAC convention): anode (oxidation) on the left, cathode on the right; | = phase boundary, ‖ = salt bridge.

Zn(s) | Zn²⁺(aq) ‖ Cu²⁺(aq) | Cu(s)

When both species in a half-cell are ions (e.g. Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺), an inert platinum electrode is used: Pt(s) | Fe²⁺(aq), Fe³⁺(aq).

In the Cu/Ag cell above (voltmeter 0.46 V), which statement is correct?

  1. Silver is the anode
  2. Electrons flow from silver to copper through the wire
  3. Copper is oxidized and is the negative electrode
  4. Electrons flow through the salt bridge

Copper is more reactive than silver, so Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ at the anode (−). Electrons flow from Cu to Ag in the wire, where Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag. Only ions move in the salt bridge.

R3.2.6 Primary cells

A primary cell is a voltaic cell designed to be used once and then discarded: its redox reaction cannot be easily reversed. Examples are alkaline (zinc/manganese(IV) oxide) cells and zinc–carbon dry cells. Zinc is oxidized at the anode in both. Cells using reactive metals such as lithium give a larger voltage and a lighter cell.

A fuel cell is a voltaic cell in which the reactants (e.g. H₂ and O₂, or methanol) are supplied continuously, so it does not run down (see R1.3). In an acidic hydrogen fuel cell: anode H₂ → 2H⁺ + 2e⁻; cathode O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O; overall 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O.

R3.2.7 Secondary (rechargeable) cells

In a secondary cell the redox reaction is reversible. During discharge it acts as a voltaic cell; during recharging an external power supply forces the reaction backwards, so it acts as an electrolytic cell.

CellKey featuresUses
Lead–acidPb anode, PbO₂ cathode, H₂SO₄ electrolyte; both electrodes form PbSO₄ on discharge. Heavy; toxic lead and corrosive acid.car batteries
Lithium-ionLi⁺ ions move between a graphite electrode and a metal-oxide electrode (e.g. LiCoO₂). Light, high energy density, but flammable electrolyte and limited lithium/cobalt resources.phones, laptops, electric cars
Nickel–cadmium / nickel–metal hydrideNi-based cathode; Cd is toxic, NiMH less so.older rechargeables, hybrid cars

Evaluating cells: compare voltage, energy density, lifetime/number of charge cycles, cost, safety and environmental impact (mining, toxic metals, recycling).

Which describes a secondary cell while it is being recharged?

  1. A voltaic cell converting chemical to electrical energy
  2. An electrolytic cell driving a non-spontaneous reaction
  3. A fuel cell
  4. A primary cell

Recharging uses an external supply to force the discharge reaction backwards – the definition of electrolysis.

R3.2.8 Electrolytic cells

DefinitionAn electrolytic cell uses electrical energy from an external power supply to drive a non-spontaneous redox reaction. The electrolyte is an ionic compound that is molten or dissolved, so its ions are free to move.
  • The cathode is connected to the negative terminal; cations move to it and are reduced.
  • The anode is connected to the positive terminal; anions move to it and are oxidized.
  • Electrons travel in the external circuit; current is carried through the electrolyte by moving ions.
  • Electrodes are usually inert (graphite or platinum).

Mnemonic: cat-ions are paws-itive and go to the cathode.

Worked exampleElectrolysis of molten lead(II) bromide with graphite electrodes.
  • Cathode (−): Pb²⁺(l) + 2e⁻ → Pb(l)   grey molten metal
  • Anode (+): 2Br⁻(l) → Br₂(g) + 2e⁻   brown vapour
  • Overall: PbBr₂(l) → Pb(l) + Br₂(g)
Molten NaCl: cathode Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na; anode 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻. A molten binary salt always gives the metal at the cathode and the non-metal at the anode.
Predict the products of electrolysing these molten salts: KI, CaO, LiF, MgCl₂, BeBr₂, CaCl₂
Molten saltAnode (+)Cathode (−)
KIiodine: 2I⁻ → I₂ + 2e⁻potassium: K⁺ + e⁻ → K
CaOoxygen: 2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻calcium: Ca²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Ca
LiFfluorine: 2F⁻ → F₂ + 2e⁻lithium
MgCl₂chlorinemagnesium
BeBr₂bromineberyllium
CaCl₂chlorinecalcium

State symbols for molten electrolytes are (l), not (aq).

Voltaic cellElectrolytic cell
Energy changechemical → electricalelectrical → chemical
Reactionspontaneous (ΔG < 0)non-spontaneous (ΔG > 0)
Anodenegative; oxidationpositive; oxidation
Cathodepositive; reductionnegative; reduction
Set-uptwo half-cells and a salt bridgeone container, power supply
Common mistakeThe sign of the anode and cathode is different in the two cell types, but the process is not: oxidation is always at the anode and reduction always at the cathode.

In the electrolysis of molten sodium chloride, what happens at the positive electrode?

  1. Na⁺ ions are reduced
  2. Cl⁻ ions are oxidized
  3. Na⁺ ions are oxidized
  4. Cl⁻ ions are reduced

In an electrolytic cell the positive electrode is the anode. Anions are attracted to it and lose electrons: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻.

title: Redox in organic chemistry: oxidation and reduction of functional groups
html:
R3.2.9 Oxidation of functional groups in organic compounds

In organic chemistry, oxidation usually means gaining O or losing H. The oxidizing agent is written [O]. Common oxidizing agents are acidified potassium dichromate(VI), K₂Cr₂O₇/H⁺ (made from potassium dichromate and sulfuric acid; colour change orange → green as Cr₂O₇²⁻ is reduced to Cr³⁺) and acidified potassium manganate(VII), KMnO₄/H⁺ (purple → colourless).

AlcoholProductConditions
Primary, RCH₂OHaldehyde RCHOheat and distil off the aldehyde as it forms (excess alcohol) to stop further oxidation
Primary, RCH₂OHcarboxylic acid RCOOH (via the aldehyde)heat under reflux with excess oxidizing agent
Secondary, R₁CH(OH)R₂ketone R₁COR₂heat (reflux); ketones are not oxidized further
Tertiaryno reactiondichromate stays orange – no H on the carbon bonded to OH
CH₃CH₂OH + [O] → CH₃CHO + H₂O     CH₃CHO + [O] → CH₃COOH
CH₃CH(OH)CH₃ + [O] → CH₃COCH₃ + H₂O    (propan-2-ol → propanone)

Look at what happens to the atoms: in RCH₂OH → RCHO the O–H hydrogen and one C–H hydrogen are removed and a C=O double bond forms; in RCHO → RCOOH an O atom is inserted into the aldehyde C–H bond. Aldehydes have a C=O at the end of the chain (suffix -al), ketones have C=O within the chain (-one), and carboxylic acids have C=O and OH on the same terminal carbon (-oic acid).

Distillation works because the aldehyde has a lower boiling point than the alcohol and acid (no hydrogen bonding between aldehyde molecules), so it escapes before it can be oxidized further. Reflux keeps volatile components in the flask long enough for complete oxidation; the vapour condenses and drips back. Use an electric heater or water bath, not an open flame – organic vapours are flammable. The acid is then separated by distillation.

Exam tipDistinguish aldehydes and ketones: an aldehyde can still be oxidized, so it turns warm acidified dichromate from orange to green, gives a brick-red precipitate with Fehling's solution (blue → brick red) and a silver mirror with Tollens' reagent (colourless → silver). A ketone gives none of these. Combustion also oxidizes alcohols but destroys the carbon skeleton.

Which alcohol does not change the colour of warm acidified potassium dichromate(VI)?

  1. ethanol
  2. propan-2-ol
  3. 2-methylpropan-2-ol
  4. butan-1-ol

2-methylpropan-2-ol is tertiary: the carbon bearing OH has no H atom, so it cannot be oxidized and the solution stays orange.

How would you make ethanal (not ethanoic acid) from ethanol?

  1. Reflux with excess acidified dichromate
  2. Heat with acidified dichromate and distil the product off immediately, using excess ethanol
  3. Add NaBH₄
  4. Heat with H₂ and Ni

Distilling removes the aldehyde as it forms, and limiting the oxidizing agent prevents further oxidation to the acid.

Do now: draw the steps for the complete oxidation of ethanol and of propan-2-ol.

Ethanol → ethanal (CH₃CHO) → ethanoic acid (CH₃COOH): two oxidation steps, so reflux with excess oxidizing agent. Propan-2-ol → propanone (CH₃COCH₃): one step only; the ketone is not oxidized further.

R3.2.10 Reduction of functional groups

Reduction (gain of H) reverses these oxidations. Reducing agents supply hydride ions, H⁻ (H in oxidation state −1); the reducing agent is written [H].

  • Lithium aluminium hydride, LiAlH₄ (in dry ether, then water/acid): strong; reduces carboxylic acids → aldehydes → primary alcohols. The aldehyde cannot be isolated because it is reduced faster than the acid. Water must be excluded during the first stage because H⁻ reacts with water (and any H⁺) to form H₂.
  • Sodium borohydride, NaBH₄ (in water or alcohol): milder; reduces aldehydes → primary alcohols and ketones → secondary alcohols, but not carboxylic acids.
RCOOH + 2[H] → RCHO + H₂O    RCHO + 2[H] → RCH₂OH    R₁COR₂ + 2[H] → R₁CH(OH)R₂

The C=O bond is strongly polar (O is more electronegative), so the carbonyl carbon is δ+ and is attacked by the H⁻ nucleophile; the planar C=O can be attacked from either face. Water (or dilute acid) then supplies H⁺ to the negatively charged oxygen.

LiAlH₄ is stronger than NaBH₄ because the Al–H bond is more polar than B–H (larger electronegativity difference), so H⁻ is released more readily. The smaller Li⁺ ion (higher charge density) also polarizes the C=O bond more. Hydride reagents attack the polar C=O bond but do not reduce a non-polar C=C bond.

Why does NaBH₄ not reduce carboxylic acids? The acid's O–H proton reacts with the hydride (making H₂), and the resulting carboxylate ion is negatively charged and repels the H⁻ nucleophile – only the much stronger LiAlH₄ succeeds.

Which reagent reduces butanoic acid to butan-1-ol?

  1. NaBH₄ in water
  2. LiAlH₄ in dry ether, then dilute acid
  3. H₂ with a Ni catalyst
  4. Acidified K₂Cr₂O₇

Only LiAlH₄ is strong enough to reduce a carboxylic acid. Dichromate is an oxidizing agent; Ni/H₂ reduces C=C, not COOH.

An unsaturated aldehyde CH₂=CHCHO is treated with NaBH₄. What is the product?

  1. CH₃CH₂CHO
  2. CH₂=CHCH₂OH
  3. CH₃CH₂CH₂OH
  4. CH₂=CHCOOH

NaBH₄ reduces the polar C=O to CH₂OH but leaves the non-polar C=C untouched. H₂/Ni would reduce the C=C.

R3.2.11 Reduction of unsaturated compounds

Alkenes and alkynes are reduced by hydrogen gas with a catalyst (finely divided nickel at about 150 °C, or Pt/Pd at room temperature). This is an addition (hydrogenation) reaction.

CH₂=CH₂ + H₂ → CH₃CH₃     HC≡CH + 2H₂ → CH₃CH₃ (via CH₂=CH₂)

Uses: converting liquid vegetable oils into solid fats (margarine). Partial hydrogenation can produce unhealthy trans fats.

Write equations for the reactions of hydrogen with: ethyne, propene, but-2-ene, but-2-yne, oct-4-ene
  • HC≡CH + 2H₂ → CH₃CH₃
  • CH₂=CHCH₃ + H₂ → CH₃CH₂CH₃
  • CH₃CH=CHCH₃ + H₂ → CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃
  • CH₃C≡CCH₃ + 2H₂ → CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃
  • CH₃(CH₂)₂CH=CH(CH₂)₂CH₃ + H₂ → CH₃(CH₂)₆CH₃ (octane)

How many moles of H₂ are needed to fully hydrogenate 1 mol of hexa-1,3-diene?

Two C=C bonds, each adding one H₂: 2 mol.

title: Standard electrode potentials, E°cell and ΔG° (AHL)
html:
R3.2.12 Standard electrode potentials and the standard hydrogen electrode AHL

A voltaic cell generates an electromotive force (EMF), the cell potential E, which drives electrons from the anode (−) to the cathode (+) through the external circuit. Because only potential differences can be measured, every half-cell is measured against a reference: the standard hydrogen electrode (SHE), assigned E° = 0.00 V.

DefinitionThe SHE consists of hydrogen gas at 100 kPa bubbled over an inert platinum electrode (coated in platinum black) dipping into a solution of H⁺(aq) at 1.00 mol dm⁻³, at 298 K: 2H⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ ⇌ H₂(g), E° = 0.00 V.
The standard electrode potential, E°, of a half-cell is the potential difference between that half-cell and the SHE under standard conditions (298 K, 100 kPa, 1.00 mol dm⁻³ solutions).

Platinum is used because it is inert and conducts, and provides a surface for the H₂/H⁺ equilibrium. In a cell diagram the SHE is written Pt(s) | H₂(g) | H⁺(aq). Standard conditions matter because concentration, pressure and temperature shift the position of each redox equilibrium: for Mⁿ⁺(aq) + ne⁻ ⇌ M(s), increasing [Mⁿ⁺] shifts it right and makes the potential more positive.

E° values are always written for the reduction half-equation (data booklet section on standard electrode potentials):

Half-equation (reduction)E° / V
Li⁺ + e⁻ ⇌ Li−3.04
Na⁺ + e⁻ ⇌ Na−2.71
Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻ ⇌ Mg−2.37
Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ ⇌ Al−1.66
2H₂O + 2e⁻ ⇌ H₂ + 2OH⁻−0.83
Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ ⇌ Zn−0.76
Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻ ⇌ Fe−0.45
Ni²⁺ + 2e⁻ ⇌ Ni−0.26
2H⁺ + 2e⁻ ⇌ H₂0.00
Sn⁴⁺ + 2e⁻ ⇌ Sn²⁺+0.15
Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ ⇌ Cu+0.34
I₂ + 2e⁻ ⇌ 2I⁻+0.54
Fe³⁺ + e⁻ ⇌ Fe²⁺+0.77
Ag⁺ + e⁻ ⇌ Ag+0.80
Br₂ + 2e⁻ ⇌ 2Br⁻+1.09
O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ ⇌ 2H₂O+1.23
Cl₂ + 2e⁻ ⇌ 2Cl⁻+1.36
MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ ⇌ Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O+1.51
F₂ + 2e⁻ ⇌ 2F⁻+2.87
  • More positive E°: the left-hand species is more easily reduced → stronger oxidizing agent (F₂ is the strongest).
  • More negative E°: the right-hand species is more easily oxidized → stronger reducing agent (Li is the strongest).
  • E° values do not depend on how many times the equation is multiplied (do not double E° when you double a half-equation).

Using the table, which is the strongest reducing agent: Zn, Fe²⁺, I⁻ or Cu?

  1. Zn
  2. Fe²⁺
  3. I⁻
  4. Cu

A reducing agent is on the right of a half-equation. The more negative the E°, the more easily the right-hand species is oxidized: Zn (−0.76 V) beats Cu (+0.34), I⁻ (+0.54) and Fe²⁺ (+0.77).

R3.2.13 Calculating E°cell and predicting spontaneity AHL

E°cell = E°(cathode, reduction) − E°(anode, oxidation)    = E°(more positive) − E°(more negative)    (Erhs − Elhs of the cell diagram)

In a voltaic cell the half-cell with the more negative E° is the anode (its reaction runs backwards, as oxidation) and the more positive one is the cathode. A positive E°cell means the reaction is spontaneous as written. For the Daniell cell, E°cell = +0.34 − (−0.76) = +1.10 V, which is what the voltmeter reads.

Worked exampleA cell is made from Mg²⁺/Mg (−2.37 V) and Ag⁺/Ag (+0.80 V).
  1. Mg has the more negative E°, so Mg is oxidized (anode, −): Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻.
  2. Ag⁺ is reduced (cathode, +): Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag. Double it to match electrons.
  3. Overall: Mg(s) + 2Ag⁺(aq) → Mg²⁺(aq) + 2Ag(s).
  4. E°cell = +0.80 − (−2.37) = +3.17 V (not doubled).
  5. Cell diagram: Mg(s) | Mg²⁺(aq) ‖ Ag⁺(aq) | Ag(s).

Calculate E°cell for Mg(s) | Mg²⁺(aq) ‖ Cu²⁺(aq) | Cu(s).

E°cell = E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) − E°(Mg²⁺/Mg) = +0.34 − (−2.37) = +2.71 V.

A Mg(s)/Mg²⁺(aq) half-cell is connected to a Ni(s)/Ni²⁺(aq) half-cell. Calculate the standard EMF.

Mg (−2.37 V) is oxidized; Ni²⁺ (−0.26 V) is reduced. E°cell = −0.26 − (−2.37) = +2.11 V. Cell: Mg(s) | Mg²⁺(aq) ‖ Ni²⁺(aq) | Ni(s); overall Mg + Ni²⁺ → Mg²⁺ + Ni.

Is a reaction feasible? Identify which species is reduced and which oxidized as written, then calculate E° = E°(reduced species' half-cell) − E°(oxidized species' half-cell). Positive → spontaneous; negative → not spontaneous (the reverse reaction is).

Worked exampleWill chlorine oxidize iodide ions? Will iodine oxidize chloride ions?
  • Cl₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + I₂: E° = +1.36 − (+0.54) = +0.82 V → spontaneous.
  • I₂ + 2Cl⁻ → 2I⁻ + Cl₂: E° = +0.54 − (+1.36) = −0.82 V → not spontaneous.
Will zinc react with 1 mol dm⁻³ HCl? Zn + 2H⁺ → Zn²⁺ + H₂: E° = 0.00 − (−0.76) = +0.76 V → yes. Copper: E° = 0.00 − 0.34 = −0.34 V → no.
Worked exampleExplain why fluorine reacts with water, and write the equation.
  • E°(F₂/F⁻) = +2.87 V > E°(O₂/H₂O) = +1.23 V, so F₂ is reduced and water is oxidized to O₂.
  • 2F₂(g) + 2H₂O(l) → 4F⁻(aq) + O₂(g) + 4H⁺(aq); E°cell = 2.87 − 1.23 = +1.64 V.
By the same argument chlorine (+1.36 V) should oxidize water (+1.23 V): 2Cl₂ + 2H₂O → 4Cl⁻ + O₂ + 4H⁺, although the reaction is slow.

Can tin(II) ions reduce iron(III) ions? Calculate E° for Sn²⁺ + 2Fe³⁺ → Sn⁴⁺ + 2Fe²⁺ (E°(Sn⁴⁺/Sn²⁺) = +0.15 V).

Fe³⁺ is reduced (+0.77 V), Sn²⁺ is oxidized (+0.15 V): E° = 0.77 − 0.15 = +0.62 V. Positive, so yes, the reaction is spontaneous.

Hydrogen gas is bubbled into a solution containing Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺ ions (standard conditions). What happens?

  1. Nothing
  2. Fe³⁺ is reduced to Fe²⁺ and H₂ is oxidized to H⁺
  3. Fe²⁺ is reduced to Fe
  4. Fe²⁺ is oxidized to Fe³⁺

E°(Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺) = +0.77 V > E°(H⁺/H₂) = 0.00 V, so 2Fe³⁺ + H₂ → 2Fe²⁺ + 2H⁺ (E° = +0.77 V). Reducing Fe²⁺ to Fe (−0.45 V) would have a negative E°.

Exam tipShortcut: a species on the left of a half-equation will oxidize any species on the right of a half-equation with a more negative E° ("anticlockwise rule" when the table is listed with most negative at the top). E° only predicts thermodynamic feasibility; a feasible reaction can still be very slow (high Ea), and non-standard conditions change the actual potential.

R3.2.14 Standard Gibbs energy change and E°cell AHL

ΔG° = −nFE°cell
  • n = number of moles of electrons transferred in the balanced equation; F = Faraday constant = 96 500 C mol⁻¹ (data booklet); E° in volts. ΔG° comes out in J mol⁻¹ – divide by 1000 for kJ mol⁻¹.
  • E°cell > 0 ⇒ ΔG° < 0 ⇒ spontaneous. E°cell < 0 ⇒ ΔG° > 0 ⇒ non-spontaneous. E° = 0 ⇒ ΔG° = 0 (equilibrium).
  • Links to R1.4 and R2.3: ΔG° = −RT ln K, so a large positive E° means a very large equilibrium constant.
Worked exampleCalculate ΔG° for the Daniell cell, Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu, E° = +1.10 V.
  1. n = 2 (two electrons transferred).
  2. ΔG° = −2 × 96 500 × 1.10 = −212 300 J mol⁻¹ = −212 kJ mol⁻¹. Negative, so spontaneous.
Worked exampleFor Mg + 2Ag⁺ → Mg²⁺ + 2Ag (E° = +3.17 V), n = 2: ΔG° = −2 × 96 500 × 3.17 = −612 kJ mol⁻¹.

For Mg + Ni²⁺ → Mg²⁺ + Ni (E° = +2.11 V), calculate ΔG° in kJ mol⁻¹.

ΔG° = −2 × 96 500 × 2.11 = −407 230 J mol⁻¹ = −407 kJ mol⁻¹.

A cell is made from Ni²⁺/Ni (−0.26 V) and Ag⁺/Ag (+0.80 V). Calculate ΔG° (kJ mol⁻¹) for Ni + 2Ag⁺ → Ni²⁺ + 2Ag.

E°cell = 0.80 − (−0.26) = +1.06 V; n = 2. ΔG° = −2 × 96 500 × 1.06 = −204 580 J mol⁻¹ ≈ −205 kJ mol⁻¹. Silver is the positive electrode.
Why does ΔG become zero when a cell "goes flat"?

As the cell discharges, reactant concentrations fall and product concentrations rise until the system reaches equilibrium. At equilibrium the forward and reverse rates are equal, the EMF is zero and so ΔG = −nFE = 0. (The position of that equilibrium lies far to the right, because K is very large.)

Show that copper(I) ions disproportionate in water (E°(Cu⁺/Cu) = +0.52 V, E°(Cu²⁺/Cu⁺) = +0.15 V).

Half-equations: Cu⁺ + e⁻ → Cu (reduction, +0.52 V) and Cu⁺ → Cu²⁺ + e⁻ (oxidation of the +0.15 V couple). Overall 2Cu⁺(aq) → Cu(s) + Cu²⁺(aq); E° = 0.52 − 0.15 = +0.37 V > 0, so it is spontaneous. Copper goes from +1 to 0 and +2.

title: Electrolysis of aqueous solutions and electroplating (AHL)
html:
R3.2.15 Electrolysis of aqueous solutions AHL

In aqueous solution, water can also be oxidized or reduced, so it competes with the ions of the solute:

cathode: 2H₂O(l) + 2e⁻ → H₂(g) + 2OH⁻(aq)   E° = −0.83 V
anode: 2H₂O(l) → O₂(g) + 4H⁺(aq) + 4e⁻   (reverse of E° = +1.23 V)

Which product forms depends on three factors:

  1. E° values: at the cathode, the species with the more positive E° is reduced; at the anode, the species with the less positive (more negative) E° is oxidized.
  2. Concentration: a high concentration of an ion favours its discharge (e.g. concentrated Cl⁻ gives Cl₂ even though E°(Cl₂) is slightly more positive than E°(O₂)).
  3. Electrode material: active electrodes (e.g. copper) can themselves be oxidized at the anode.
Key pointPractical rules. Cathode: metals below hydrogen in the activity series (Cu, Ag) are deposited; for reactive metals (group 1, group 2, Al) H₂ is produced instead. Anode (inert): concentrated halide ions (Cl⁻, Br⁻, I⁻) give the halogen; otherwise (SO₄²⁻, NO₃⁻, F⁻, dilute Cl⁻) O₂ is produced from water.
Electrolyte (inert electrodes)Cathode productAnode productSolution afterwards
Concentrated NaCl(aq)H₂Cl₂NaOH(aq) forms
Very dilute NaCl(aq)H₂O₂ (mainly)more concentrated NaCl
CuSO₄(aq)CuO₂becomes acidic (H₂SO₄), blue fades
Na₂SO₄(aq) or dilute H₂SO₄ (electrolysis of water)H₂O₂H₂ : O₂ volume ratio 2 : 1
KI(aq)H₂I₂KOH(aq) forms
CuSO₄(aq) with copper electrodesCu depositedCu anode dissolves (Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻)unchanged [Cu²⁺], blue colour stays
Worked exampleExplain the products of electrolysing concentrated aqueous sodium chloride with inert electrodes.
  • Cathode: Na⁺ (E° −2.71 V) vs H₂O (E° −0.83 V). Water has the more positive E°, so it is reduced: 2H₂O + 2e⁻ → H₂ + 2OH⁻.
  • Anode: Cl⁻ (+1.36 V) vs H₂O (+1.23 V). The values are close, and the high [Cl⁻] makes chlorine discharge favourable: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻.
  • Na⁺ and OH⁻ remain, so the solution becomes sodium hydroxide (the basis of the chlor-alkali industry).

Note that the electrolysis of molten NaCl gives sodium, but aqueous NaCl never does – a classic exam contrast.

Aqueous lithium fluoride is electrolysed with inert electrodes. What forms at the anode?

  1. Fluorine
  2. Oxygen
  3. Hydrogen
  4. Lithium

F⁻ is almost impossible to oxidize (E°(F₂/F⁻) = +2.87 V), so water is oxidized instead: 2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻. Fluorine is only obtained from molten fluorides. Hydrogen forms at the cathode.

Which pair of products forms when aqueous potassium iodide is electrolysed with inert electrodes?

  1. K at cathode, I₂ at anode
  2. H₂ at cathode, I₂ at anode
  3. H₂ at cathode, O₂ at anode
  4. K at cathode, O₂ at anode

K⁺ is far harder to reduce than water, so H₂ forms at the cathode; I⁻ is easily oxidized (E° +0.54 V), so I₂ (brown in solution) forms at the anode.

Draw and annotate the electrolysis of copper(II) chloride solution. Where do oxidation and reduction occur?

Cu²⁺ (cation) moves to the negative cathode and is reduced: Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ → Cu(s) (pink-brown deposit). Cl⁻ (anion) moves to the positive anode and is oxidized: 2Cl⁻(aq) → Cl₂(g) + 2e⁻ (bubbles of pale green gas). The ions can move because the compound is dissolved (or molten).

Two cells are connected in series: one contains CuSO₄(aq) with copper electrodes, the other dilute NaOH(aq) with Pt electrodes. The copper anode loses 0.6355 g. Calculate the total volume of gas (in dm³ at STP, 22.7 dm³ mol⁻¹) produced in the NaOH cell.

n(Cu) = 0.6355/63.55 = 0.01000 mol, so 0.02000 mol e⁻ passed through both cells. NaOH cell: cathode 2H₂O + 2e⁻ → H₂ + 2OH⁻ gives 0.01000 mol H₂; anode 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ gives 0.00500 mol O₂. Total 0.0150 mol × 22.7 = 0.341 dm³.

Electricity is passed through dilute H₂SO₄(aq) and molten PbBr₂ in series; 250 cm³ of O₂ (at STP) forms in the first cell. Calculate the mass of lead formed in the second cell (Ar(Pb) = 207.2).

n(O₂) = 0.250/22.7 = 0.0110 mol; 4 mol e⁻ per O₂ → 0.0441 mol e⁻. Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb, so n(Pb) = 0.0220 mol; m = 0.0220 × 207.2 = 4.56 g. (The same cell also makes 500 cm³ of H₂.)

R3.2.16 Electroplating AHL

Electroplating uses electrolysis to coat an object with a thin layer of metal, for decoration or corrosion resistance (silver-plated cutlery, chromium-plated taps, copper on steel), or to coat a cheaper metal with a more expensive one.

  • Cathode (−): the object to be plated. Metal ions are reduced and deposited on it: Ag⁺(aq) + e⁻ → Ag(s).
  • Anode (+): a piece of the plating metal, which dissolves: Ag(s) → Ag⁺(aq) + e⁻.
  • Electrolyte: a solution containing ions of the plating metal (e.g. AgNO₃(aq), CuSO₄(aq)).
  • The anode replaces the ions removed at the cathode, so the electrolyte concentration (and colour) stays constant.

Class practical: copper-plate a coin or paperclip. Connect the object to the negative terminal of a 6 V supply and a copper strip to the positive terminal, both dipping into 0.5 mol dm⁻³ CuSO₄(aq) (harmful – wear goggles). After 1–2 minutes the object is coated pink-brown. Cathode: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu; anode: Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻.

The same arrangement with an impure copper anode and pure copper cathode is used to purify copper: copper dissolves from the anode and deposits as pure copper on the cathode, while unreactive impurities fall as anode sludge.

Exam tipFor a good, even coating: clean the object, use a low current, keep the electrolyte concentration constant and allow time. The mass deposited is proportional to the charge passed (current × time).

To silver-plate a steel spoon, which arrangement is correct?

  1. Spoon as anode, silver as cathode, AgNO₃(aq)
  2. Spoon as cathode, silver as anode, AgNO₃(aq)
  3. Spoon as cathode, graphite anode, NaCl(aq)
  4. Spoon as anode, silver as cathode, NaNO₃(aq)

Ag⁺ must be reduced on the spoon, so the spoon is the negative cathode. The silver anode dissolves to replace the Ag⁺ used, so the electrolyte must contain Ag⁺.

In electroplating the object to be coated is always the cathode, and the electrolyte must contain ions of the plating metal.
